stage: S3 one linear layer, four splits
basis: S1 measured 44.3 GB/s cross-card copy; S4 measured 63.9 us/layer for the same 8704x5120 bf16 GEMV and 8.3-8.7 us for a 10 KiB all-reduce. Predictions below are ESTIMATES from those components, not from this run.
question: At which batch size does splitting one [N,K] layer across two cards stop paying, and does split-N beat split-K?

variants.split_n: each card half of N (4352), then SUM all-reduce of its [M,4352] output; combine is concatenation, so the collective is timed but its arithmetic is unused; correctness compares each slice
variants.split_k: each card half of K (2560, contiguous copy), full [M,N] partial, SUM all-reduce gives the exact result
variants.single_split_k: one card computes both K halves locally and adds them: split cost without a collective

crossover_prediction: split-N stays at or below single-card through M=4096, because its payload grows at the same M rate as the compute it replaces; split-K loses once its doubled payload (M*8704*2) stops being negligible, expected first at M=512-4096.
quantization: int4 is NOT tested: no int4 GEMV kernel is installed, and emulating it would measure a different kernel. The manual's claim that int4 loses sooner stays untested and is recorded as such.
decision_rule: Split wins when measured split <= single. Report every cell; do not select the best batch. If split-N does not win at M=1, the TP premise fails at this shape and S6 must be re-argued before any model work.
correctness: single is the reference. split_n compares each card's half against the reference slice; split_k compares the summed partials. BF16 tolerance: exact slices are not required, max abs difference and allclose(rtol=1e-2,atol=1e-2) are recorded. The split_k contiguous copies are laid out per card so both splits read contiguous bytes.
